facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human-rights violations.
On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
While the applicant was trying to attend to the injured woman, he was beaten with clubs about the head and body by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was led away at gunpoint through an angry crowd that shouted abuse and threats on 19 July 1989.
The applicant was taken by bus to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage' on 19 July 1989.
In the morning of 20 July 1989, the applicant was taken to Seray Police Station and put in a cell that was dark, damp and dirty.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days after the court appearance on 20 July 1989.

On 22 July 1989, the applicant was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cyprus pounds (approximately 85 euros), with five additional days in prison in default of payment within 24 hours.
On 28 July 1989, the applicant was released and taken back to southern Cyprus.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that on 21 July 1989, the UN Secretary General expressed his concern at the events and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone and their responsibility to ensure that the area was not violated.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained, asking all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps to bring about a relaxation of tension.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human-rights violations.
During the afternoon of 19 July 1989, the radio announced that Turkish soldiers and policemen had started to cruelly beat the demonstrators.
The applicant was a nursing officer.
The applicant took with him a special bag containing first-aid equipment when he went to the demonstration area on 19 July 1989.
The applicant wore an armband marked with the Red Cross sign when he went to the demonstration area on 19 July 1989.
The applicant told UN officers that he was a nurse on 19 July 1989.
UN officers informed the applicant that they needed his help for a woman who had received an injury to the head and was lying on the ground.
While the applicant was trying to attend to the injured woman, he was beaten with clubs about the head and body by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
Despite the applicant's attempts to explain that he was a nurse, Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control continued to hit him.
The applicant felt a powerful blow to the head and started bleeding during the events of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was led away at gunpoint through an angry crowd that shouted abuse and threats on 19 July 1989.
The crowd had encircled the bus transporting the applicant and was hitting it with sticks and throwing stones at the arrested persons.
At the 'Pavlides Garage', a body search was carried out and all the applicant's personal effects were taken.
At the 'Pavlides Garage', the crowd was shouting and throwing stones at the garage, some of which came through the roof.
Some hours after arriving at the 'Pavlides Garage', the applicant was taken to hospital where he had stitches to his head.
The applicant was still bleeding and his clothes were soaked with blood when he was taken back to the 'Pavlides Garage'.
Sometime after midnight on 19-20 July 1989, the applicant was interrogated by a Greek-speaking officer at the 'Pavlides Garage'.
The applicant declared during interrogation that he had joined the demonstration voluntarily for humanitarian reasons.
The applicant was told to sign a statement in Turkish but refused, as he did not understand Turkish.
The applicant refused to sign the statement in Turkish because signing would have been tantamount to recognising the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' (the 'TRNC').
In the morning of 20 July 1989, the applicant was taken to Seray Police Station and put in a cell that was dark, damp and dirty.
While at Seray Police Station, the applicant was beaten and threatened.
The applicant informed the judge on 20 July 1989 that he had attended the demonstration only in order to offer humanitarian aid as a member of the Red Cross.
The court remained completely indifferent to what the applicant said on 20 July 1989.
At Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was blindfolded and led to another area of the prison where he was interrogated and punched.
The interrogation at Ortakeuy Prison was aimed solely at eliciting military information and the applicant lied about certain details.
The applicant was forced to wash the blood from his clothes before appearing in court the next day.
The accused had no legal representation at the court hearing on 21 July 1989.
The quality of the interpretation at the court hearing on 21 July 1989 was poor; the applicant felt that the interpreter was not translating all of what was being said.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the Bishop of Kitium spoke on behalf of the other accused and said that they would agree to be defended only by a Greek-Cypriot or UN lawyer.
The judge at the court hearing on 21 July 1989 replied that she could only appoint a lawyer registered with the 'TRNC' bar association.
The accused pleaded not guilty at the court hearing on 21 July 1989 and stated that they did not recognise the legitimacy of the 'TRNC' or its tribunals.
The judge refused to allow some of the questions put by the Bishop of Kitium to the first prosecution witness, and the Bishop accordingly declined to cross-examine any other witness.
The prosecution witnesses lied about basic facts surrounding the demonstration and the arrest of the accused at the court hearing on 21 July 1989.
One of the persons present in the courtroom on 21 July 1989 spoke briefly to the Bishop of Kitium, who became frightened as a result.
A hostile crowd gathered outside the courtroom on 22 July 1989.
An angry crowd had assembled within the precinct of the court on 22 July 1989 and was shouting, swearing and making obscene gestures at the accused.
The applicant had the impression that the crowd's presence and actions on 22 July 1989 were being orchestrated and controlled by the police.

From 24 until 28 July 1989, the applicant went on a hunger strike to protest about the prison director's refusal to give the Bishop of Kitium church vestments and holy vessels with which to celebrate mass.
The applicant was put in an isolation cell as punishment for going on hunger strike.
In support of his claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced a medical certificate issued on 29 July 1989 by Dr A. Hadjihannas, a medical officer at Nicosia Hospital.

The medical certificate issued on 29 July 1989 by Dr A. Hadjihannas states that Dr Hadjihannas examined the applicant (Costas Stratis) on 29 July 1989 and found a head injury to the left frontal bone with four stitches.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment on 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters and were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the events of 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.
In his report of 7 December 1989 on UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that a serious situation arose in July 1989 as a result of a demonstration by Greek Cypriots in Nicosia.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that a short while later, Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators, whose number fluctuated between 200 and 2,000, blocked all UN traffic through the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in the island and intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.
The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the UN Secretary General urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that on 24 July 1989, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties the Security Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained, asking all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps to bring about a relaxation of tension.
The applicant produced 21 photographs taken at different times during the demonstration on 19 July 1989.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the demonstrators during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the accused did not accept the charges against them and stated that they did not wish to use the services of a lawyer registered in the 'TRNC'.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the prosecution witnesses (mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration) declared that the accused had illegally crossed the 'TRNC' border, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that knives and other cutting objects had been found in the bags of some of the demonstrators who had been arrested.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the accused had been told that they could cross-examine witnesses in turn and, if they so wished, choose one of their number to cross-examine the witnesses on behalf of all the accused.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that during the hearing of evidence, one of the accused put a few questions to one of the prosecution witnesses.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the applicant had stated that he considered the Cypriot coast to be the border and for that reason did not accept that he had violated the border.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that before the District Court gave its sentence, the Bishop of Kitium, speaking on behalf of all the accused, made a statement saying that their struggle had been peaceful, that their aim was to have Greek-Cypriots and Turkish-Cypriots living together in peace, that they had not been carrying weapons and that they had asked for UN protection.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded, relying on statements by the prosecution witnesses, that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused were guilty on both counts.

In deciding on the sentence, the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the 'TRNC'.
